title: Ramadan: the whole book
hookLine: finishing the Qur'an in the month, one juz' a night

lines: THE LAST PAGES, ON A LATE NIGHT.
THE KHATM: THE WHOLE BOOK HEARD.
cards: On one of the last nights of Ramadan, in many mosques, something happens that the regulars have been waiting for all month. The imam reaches the final pages of the Qur'an. The short surahs at the end.

Then the very last one, An-Nas. And then, in many places, a long supplication, the khatm, with people in tears, because they've just heard the whole book, start to finish, standing in rows night after night.
It started on the month's first night, with one portion. Today, how a book gets finished.

teach.b: The Qur'an is divided, for reading, into thirty parts of roughly equal length. Each one is a juz'. The divisions don't come from the revelation itself.

They were added later as a reading aid, and they're marked in the margins of many printed copies. Thirty parts, one a day, make a month. Many copies also divide each juz' into two halves, each called a hizb.

So when a mosque recites one juz' a night in the tarawih prayers, it finishes the whole book by the end of Ramadan. Some do the same alone, a juz' a day, in the morning before work or at night after the fast.
How fast should anyone read? Bukhari records the young companion 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr wanting to recite the whole Qur'an far more often. The Prophet ﷺ told him: read it in a month.
He said he could do more.

teach.h: READ IT IN SEVEN, AND NO LESS.
teach.b: In the end the Prophet said: then read it in seven, and no less. Another report says that one who reads it in less than three days hasn't understood it.
And the Qur'an itself, in Surah Al-Muzzammil, tells the Prophet: "and chant the Qur'an in measure." Tartil, the word is: unhurried, each letter given its due. So the goal isn't speed.
It's a steady pace that carries you to the end. One juz' a night. Thirty steps.
Then, on a late night near the end, the last page turns.

how: Many mosques recite one juz' a night in the tarawih prayers to complete the Qur'an by the end of Ramadan, often closing with a khatm supplication, and many Muslims read a juz' a day at home.

games.q: you're young and eager. you tell the Prophet you want to read the whole Qur'an every day. what does he say?
o: read it in a month; if you must go faster, in seven days, and no less.
games.why: a month, he said. 'Abdullah pushed for more, and was told: then in seven, and no less.

practice: Think of something long you've started: a book, a course, a habit, maybe this path. Picture where you began, where you are now, and the end.
If you read the Qur'an, mark the place you've reached with a ribbon or a note; if not, mark your place in whatever long thing you're doing.

wordCard.voice: Ramadan again: the month when many Muslims hear or read the whole Qur'an, one juz', one thirtieth, each night. Today's word.
